PROJECT RATING DATE: The project rating date is the evaluation date the project credit rating will be derived. The information below must be captured and based on the date above. For calibration purposes this date should be the same for all the project finance deals captured. This input denotes the evaluation / rating date for the project. (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy))

1.1: This sub-section refers to the variables required to assist in determining the value of the project over the life of the loan.

In the event of default, what is the liq: This input denotes the approximate liquidation costs in the case of default and subsequent liquidation need to be entered as a percentage of the exposure at default (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE %). FUNDING DETAILS:: This section captures the funding details of the transaction and contains components such as interest rates, start and end dates, repayment structure, etc.
Facility Amount: This input denotes the capital balance at the original commencement date of the facility. (FORMAT: NUMERIC VALUE)
Currency of funding: This input denotes the currency of the loan facility.
Outstanding Loan Amount: This input denotes the capital balance at the rating date of the facility. (FORMAT: NUMERIC VALUE)
Residual (% facility amount): This input denotes the percentage amount of the original facility amount that will be repaid as a lump sum at maturity of the loan. (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%))
Start Date (Loan issue date): This input is the original commencement date of the facility. Please capture the inception date of the facility. (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy))
End Date (Loan maturity date): This input is the original maturity date of the facility. Please capture the maturity date of the facility. (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy))
Settlement Type: This input denotes the repayment type for the underlying facility.
Ranking relative to other Loans (Senior: This input denotes the ranking of the facilities from most senior (i.e. one) to the most junior facility (i.e. five). The most senior Loan will be captured as one and junior Loans will be captured as 2, 3,4 or 5 depending on their ranking. It is possible for two Loans to have the same ranking.
Interest Rate Type (Fixed / Floating): This input denotes the whether the interest rate is fixed, floating, fixed then floating, floating then fixed or if the fixed rate changes over time. The user needs to select the appropriate interest rate type: • Fixed – this denotes that the interest rate charge is a fixed rate. The user needs to capture the fixed interest rate; • Floating – this denotes that the interest rate charge based on a floating rate. The user needs to select the floating rate from the pre-defined drop-down list; • Fixed then floating – this denotes that the interest rate charged changes from a fixed rate to a floating rate at a pre-defined date. The user needs to capture the fixed rate, select a floating rate and capture the date the interest rate charge changes from fixed to floating; • Floating then fixed – this denotes that the interest rate charged changes from a floating rate to a fixed rate at a pre-defined date. The user needs to capture the fixed rate, select a floating rate and capture the date the interest rate charge changes from floating to fixed; or • Fixed rate changes over time – this denotes that the fixed rate changes over the life of the loan. The user needs to capture the initial fixed rate, the date the rate changes and the new fixed rate.
Reference Rate: In the case of a floating interest rate, this input denotes the reference interest rate.
Fixed Rate (per annum) (1): In the case of a fixed interest rate, this input denotes this interest rate. (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%))
Date of Change (Fixed to Floating, vice: This input denotes the date whereby the interest rate will change from fixed to floating, floating to fixed or fixed to another fixed rate, if applicable. (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy))
Compounding frequency: This input denotes the number of debt service payments per annum and the compounding frequency of interest. The user has an option to change the compounding frequency once over the life of the loan. For example, during the development phase, the interest
Interest Rate Margin over / (under) floa: This input denotes the margin / spread above or below the financing rate in the cases of floating rate loans. The spread needs to be captured as a percentage, for a margin below the reference rate, a percentage with a negative sign needs to be captured (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%)).
Bank Costs (%): This input denotes the spread above the financing rate. The bank costs needs to be captured as a percentage (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%).
Floor Rate: This input denotes the lower interest rate limit percentage where a floor will be set (i.e. minimum interest rate level) for a floating rate transaction if applicable. (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%))
Cap Rate: This input denotes the upper interest rate limit percentage where a ceiling will be set (i.e. maximum interest rate level) for a floating rate transaction if applicable. (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%))
Hedge Ratio (% of loan that accrues inte: This input denotes the portion of the loan which will be financed at a fixed rate for a floating rate exposed transaction if applicable. (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE (%))
Capital Holidays (Moratoriums): This input denotes the number of years for which no capital is settled (i.e. a moratorium on capital repayments), fully or partially (i.e. no capital repayments). (FORMAT: WHOLE NUMBER)
Interest Holidays (Moratoriums): This input is the number of years for which no interest is settled (i.e. no interest repayments), but the interest is capitalised (i.e. a moratorium on interest repayments). (FORMAT: WHOLE NUMBER)
Political Risk Insurance Payout: These inputs denote the conditions of the payout of the PRI contract. The insurance contracts will either: • payout a maximum sum insured (i.e. capped value of insurance payout) (INPUT FORMAT: numeric value); • payout a percentage of the outstanding l
Drawdown Schedule Dates: This input denotes the specific start and end dates of the drawdown of the facility.
Debt Service Dates: This input denotes the dates for the series of payments of interest and principal required on a debt over a given period of time. Please note that the dates should be captured for each Loan .
Drawdown Schedule: This input denotes the drawdown of the facility with the specific dates that the draws are made.
Debt Service (DS): This input section denotes the series of payments of interest and principal required on a debt over a given period of time. Please note that the debt service should be captured for each Loan. 1. Capital Amount These inputs denotes multiple capital repayments with specific repayment dates. The structured capital repayment table needs to be populated with capital repayment amounts (FORMAT: NUMERIC VALUE) and the related dates (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy)). 2. Total Amount These inputs denotes total repayments (capital + interest) with specific repayment dates. The total amount repayment table needs to be populated with the total repayment amounts (FORMAT: PERCENTAGE) and the related dates (FORMAT: DATE (dd/mm/yyyy)).
Systemic country risk factors: This section assesses systemic country risks impacting on the project. Generally, systemic risk will affect all entities operating within a particular jurisdiction. Systemic risks here will include transfer risk as well as sovereign risk.
A1: This section assesses systemic country risks impacting on the project. Generally, systemic risk will affect all entities operating within a particular jurisdiction. Systemic risks here will include transfer risk as well as sovereign risk.
What is the country of risk?: The relevant country of risk will generally be assigned by the country risk team. Considerations here will include the country of operation(s), the domicile of cash flows and mitigating factors such as Political Risk Insurance ("PRI"). It is important to assess whether the PRI cover here provides protection against default events (i.e. will influence the rating) or against loss in the event of default (i.e. the recovery rate). Please note that parental support should not be considered at this point. Some examples will illustrate the required input: If operations span country A and B, but cash flows reside in country B, the country of risk will be selected as country B. If, on the other hand, cash flows reside in country C, country C will be selected as the country of risk. Given the latter scenario, if the risk of default occurring is mitigated by PRI cover, the insurer being domiciled in country D, the country of risk will change to country D.

Are the project's operations exposed to: This question evaluates whether the project's operations and / or cash flows are exposed to the risk of multiple jurisdictions (countries or borders). Likelihood of government intervention /: This question assesses the likelihood of adverse changes in the political and regulatory environment in which the project operates. Examples of adverse changes here may relate to such factors as strikes, regulatory changes posing a risk to the project (e.g. environmental, taxation, labour regulation and quotas) and political violence or terrorism. Consider the historical track record and experience within the country of operation, current events and expected future developments.

Incentive for regulators / authorities t: This question considers whether the project has the support of government, regulatory authorities and the wider community. Influential stakeholder groups need to be considered here. Specifically non-financial implicit support is being addressed here. The potential responses range from all parties actively being in favour of the project's operations to some influential parties actually opposing the project and therefore potentially being a risk to the going concern assumption of the project. Strategic projects supported by, for example, government will generally face less barriers than those where some interest groups may actively oppose a project.

Exposure of project operations and logis: This question evaluates to which degree the operations of the project are exposed to current and changing environmental conditions such as for example, the weather and the physical surroundings of the project. Also, environmental factors may cause disruptions not only in operations but also in logistics in supplying a factory with raw materials. Also, some projects may be located in areas which may be prone to natural disasters such as flooding. Consider which mitigating steps the bank has taken such as insurance cover.

Exposure of operating cash flows to comp: This question assesses the degree to which operating cash flows are negatively impacted by competition. Here, the user needs to consider not only the current level of competition, but also anticipated changes in the level of competition. Whilst competition might currently be favourable, the sustainability of a project's competitive advantage may be threatened by the actions of competitors or by substitute products. Also the sources of competitive advantage (unique technology, patents, favourable supply chains, operational efficiency, etc.) may dry up. Another consideration is the ability to react to changes in the level of competition. Here one needs to consider the existing market share (e.g. Monopoly vs. perfect competition), market structure and the degree to which competition is regulated.

Anticipated demand for end-product / ser: This question assesses the degree to which operating cash flows are adversely impacted by changes in demand levels. This question should be considered independently of any off-take agreements (in the event that the off-taker may need to be replaced). Off-take agreements may mitigate demand conditions by introducing more certainty in cash flows (depending on the quality of the agreement). Considerations may relate to the product or industry life cycle. The user should also consider the sensitivity of product demand to, for example, changes in demographic or economic conditions. Some goods are highly cyclical and correlated with the business cycle. Depressed economic conditions may therefore have adverse impacts on cash flows. Other factors may relate to the ability to respond effectively to changes in demand levels, by for example adjusting production levels or sales efforts. Further considerations include the availability of alternative markets or customer bases for services.

What is the level of maintenance risk un: This question assesses the degree to which maintenance is required to sufficiently run the project's operations in a smooth manner. The expertise and skills required to perform maintenance services, the reliability of a timely response to minimise down-time (e.g. on-call availability) and the cost of the maintenance should be considered when assessing the level of maintenance risk. The degree to which a maintenance contract mitigates the risks of down-time or the costs of maintenance needs to be considered. For example, if no contract exists, this could be very costly if unforeseen events arise. The user should also consider which maintenance reserves have been formed to provide for any contingencies.

Free Cash Flow (FCF): This input (i.e. Free Cash Flow (FCF) denotes the amount of cash that the project has left over after it has paid all of its expenses, including investments. FCF is the net cash flow that is available to all investors, including equity holders and debt providers (e.g. banks). Typically this formula is used to value either a firm or a project. There are 4 formulas to calculate free cash flow to the firm (FCFF), but they should all lead to the same results: · FCFF = Net income + Non cash charges + [ Interest x ( 1 – tax rate ) ] – Fixed Capital Investment – Working Capital Investment · FCFF = [ EBIT x ( 1 – tax rate ) ] + Depreciation – Fixed Capital Investment – Working Capital Investment · FCFF = [ EBITDA x ( 1 – tax rate ) ] + ( Depreciation x tax rate ) – Fixed Capital Investment – Working Capital Investment · FCFF = Cash flow from operations + [ Interest x ( 1 – tax rate ) ] – Fixed Capital Investment The important thing in all these formulas is that net income is adjusted by: 1 adding back any non cash expenses (e.g. depreciation) since we’re trying to get to cash flow; 2 adding back interest (adjusted for tax), similar to how we do this for cash flow available for debt service (CFDS); 3 deducting the net change in working capital (difference between current assets and liabilities); and 4 the Fixed Capital Investment (e.g. capital outlay).
